title: First Word All Beings Say Bismillah Through The Language Of Their State

questions.question: What question is raised at the start of the passage about all created things?
questions.answer: It asks whether all things truly declare Allah’s name through the way they were made and how they function.

questions.question: What example is given first to help explain this idea?
questions.answer: A picture is given of one person forcing the people of a town to move and work.

questions.question: Why would a person naturally conclude that such a man was not acting by his own strength alone?
questions.answer: Because one person by himself could not reasonably control so many people, so he must be backed by higher authority and power.

questions.question: In that example, whose authority is the man understood to be using?
questions.answer: He is understood to be serving as a soldier under the rule of the state and the king.

questions.question: How is that example connected to the rest of creation?
questions.answer: In a similar way, created things carry out amazing tasks by Allah’s command, not by independent power.

questions.question: What do seeds and grains show about this truth?
questions.answer: Tiny things can produce huge trees and carry very great outcomes, which shows power far beyond themselves.

questions.question: What do trees provide that points to divine mercy?
questions.answer: They bring out fruits and benefits for people as if receiving them from Allah’s store of mercy.

questions.question: How are gardens described in terms of what they produce?
questions.answer: They are presented like places where many different foods are prepared and brought forth by divine power.

questions.question: Which animals are mentioned, and what do they give?
questions.answer: Cows, camels, sheep, and goats are mentioned, and they provide pure nourishing milk.

questions.question: What is special about the roots of plants, trees, and grasses?
questions.answer: Even though they are very soft, they pass through hard ground and rock.

questions.question: What main lesson comes from the image of soft roots entering hard rock?
questions.answer: It shows that hardness and physical obstacles are under Allah’s command.

questions.question: How does the passage challenge people who explain everything only through nature?
questions.answer: It shows them examples where weak and delicate things do what should seem impossible if nature alone were in control.

questions.question: What comparison is made between rootlets and the staff of Musa, peace be upon him?
questions.answer: The roots are compared to a tool that breaks rock by Allah’s command, showing that their effect comes from divine order.

questions.question: What point is made by mentioning thin green leaves surviving intense heat?
questions.answer: Their survival shows that heat also remains under Allah’s control and cannot act independently.

questions.question: What is the overall message of the whole passage?
questions.answer: The whole created world points to Allah’s power and mercy by carrying out its duties as if proclaiming His name.

questions.question: What claim from earlier is examined again at the beginning of this passage?
questions.answer: The claim that all beings, through their condition and actions, express dependence on Allah.

questions.question: What kind of proof method is used first in the passage?
questions.answer: It uses a simple comparison from human life to make the unseen truth easier to understand.

questions.question: In the town example, what would make people sure that the man had official backing?
questions.answer: The scale of what he does is too great for one individual, so his success points to a ruler’s support.

questions.question: What principle does this example teach before applying it to nature?
questions.answer: Great effects coming from a weak-looking agent show that the real power is behind that agent, not in it alone.

questions.question: How is this principle applied to seeds?
questions.answer: Their small size does not match the huge trees that come from them, so the result must come from Allah’s power.

questions.question: Why are trees described as if they are giving gifts to people?
questions.answer: Because they bring out useful blessings that seem like provisions sent from divine mercy.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about gardens by comparing them to cooking vessels?
questions.answer: It suggests that many kinds of food are prepared there by Allah’s creative power.

questions.question: Why is milk in these animals presented as a sign of mercy?
questions.answer: Because a pure and beneficial food comes from living creatures in a way that points to care and provision from Allah.

questions.question: What contrast is important in the description of roots?
questions.answer: Their softness is contrasted with the hardness of the earth and rock they pass through.

questions.question: What conclusion should a reader draw from that contrast?
questions.answer: The roots are not succeeding through their own natural toughness but through submission of the earth to Allah’s command.

questions.question: What two forces especially trusted by materialistic thinkers are said to be under command?
questions.answer: Heat and hardness are both said to be controlled by Allah.

questions.question: How does the mention of Prophet Musa, peace be upon him, strengthen the argument?
questions.answer: It connects what we see in roots with a known sign of divine power over rock.

questions.question: How does the mention of Prophet Ibrahim, peace be upon him, support the point about leaves?
questions.answer: It reminds the reader that fire itself can be made harmless by Allah, so heat is not independent.

questions.question: If someone says nature works by itself, how would this passage respond?
questions.answer: It would answer that the amazing works of creation show command, wisdom, and mercy from Allah rather than self-sufficient nature.

questions.question: What is being confirmed by the short question and answer at the opening of the passage?
questions.answer: It is confirming that the whole world, through its actions, points to Allah and serves by His permission.

questions.question: Why is the example of a powerful-looking person in a town persuasive?
questions.answer: Because it helps us see that when a limited being achieves a huge task, hidden authority must stand behind him.

questions.question: What does the soldier image add to the meaning of the example?
questions.answer: It shows obedience, representation, and dependence on a ruler’s power.

questions.question: According to the passage, do created things act independently?
questions.answer: No, they carry out their tasks through Allah’s naming, command, and power.

questions.question: How do seeds and grains serve as evidence for this teaching?
questions.answer: Their tiny bodies cannot explain the giant trees and heavy growth that come from them.

questions.question: What does the passage imply about the source of fruits and tree products?
questions.answer: Their real source is Allah’s mercy, even though trees are the means.

questions.question: Why are gardens described in a way that emphasizes variety?
questions.answer: To show that many different foods come forth from one earth by planned and generous divine action.

questions.question: What does the passage teach through the example of milk?
questions.answer: Allah brings a clean and life-giving nourishment through animals as a mercy for people.

questions.question: How do the roots of plants become an argument against a purely material explanation of life?
questions.answer: Their delicate structure should not be able to overcome solid barriers unless Allah makes the barriers yield.

questions.question: What does it mean that everything becomes subjected when Allah’s name is mentioned?
questions.answer: It means created things obey divine command and can be made to serve purposes beyond their apparent strength.

questions.question: Why are the philosophers criticized in this passage?
questions.answer: Because they trust blind natural causes and miss the signs of Allah’s control.

questions.question: What is the effect of comparing rootlets to Musa’s staff?
questions.answer: It makes the reader see root growth as another sign of Allah overcoming hardness.

questions.question: What does the comparison of leaves with Ibrahim, peace be upon him, suggest?
questions.answer: It suggests that intense heat cannot destroy what Allah protects.

questions.question: How do the examples in this passage move from small things to big truths?
questions.answer: They begin with ordinary parts of nature and lead the reader to recognize Allah’s rule, mercy, and power.

questions.question: State the central idea of the passage in one sentence.
questions.answer: The natural world performs astonishing works that show it operates under Allah’s command, not by its own independent power.

questions.question: What statement about all beings is examined in this passage?
questions.answer: The statement is that all beings, by their very condition, say Allah’s name.

questions.question: What everyday-style scenario is used to test whether that statement makes sense?
questions.answer: The passage asks us to imagine one person controlling a whole town and making its people work.

questions.question: What judgment would a reasonable observer make about that person?
questions.answer: The observer would decide that he must represent a ruler and act with official power.

questions.question: Why is that judgment reasonable?
questions.answer: Because the work is too large for one ordinary person to do by himself.

questions.question: After that scenario, what is the same pattern said to appear in nature?
questions.answer: Things in creation do great works that are beyond their own size and ability, showing that Allah empowers them.

questions.question: How do seeds point beyond themselves?
questions.answer: They are tiny, yet they become the starting point of massive trees and heavy growth.

questions.question: What picture does the passage give of trees serving people?
questions.answer: Trees are shown as bringing provisions to us from Allah’s mercy.

questions.question: How are gardens portrayed as places of provision?
questions.answer: They are shown like productive places where many foods are prepared for living beings.

questions.question: Why are cows, camels, sheep, and goats mentioned together?
questions.answer: They are grouped as familiar animals that provide milk as a clear sign of Allah’s care.

questions.question: What makes the roots and rootlets especially striking as signs?
questions.answer: They are soft and fragile in appearance, yet they move through solid earth and rock.

questions.question: What truth is taught by this surprising ability of roots?
questions.answer: Strength in creation does not belong only to what looks hard or powerful; Allah gives effect to whatever He wills.

questions.question: What view is the passage correcting when it speaks sharply about naturalist thinkers?
questions.answer: It is correcting the idea that nature and physical forces act on their own without divine command.

questions.question: How does the reference to the rock struck by Musa, peace be upon him, fit the argument?
questions.answer: It shows that rock can be opened when Allah commands, so roots breaking through stone are also signs of His power.

questions.question: How does the reference to fire becoming safe relate to leaves in heat?
questions.answer: It shows that burning heat cannot harm beyond what Allah allows, just as leaves can remain fresh by His command.

questions.question: What important question is answered immediately after the opening line of this passage?
questions.answer: The passage answers that it is indeed true that all beings indicate Allah’s name through their state and work.

questions.question: What human example is used before discussing plants and animals?
questions.answer: It uses the case of a single man forcing the people of a town to gather and labor.

questions.question: What hidden reality would that example reveal?
questions.answer: It would reveal that the man acts with permission and support from a ruler.

questions.question: What does this teach us about visible causes in the world?
questions.answer: Visible causes are means, while the real power belongs to Allah.

questions.question: In what way do seeds and grains appear weak but accomplish something great?
questions.answer: They are very small, yet they become the means for huge trees and heavy produce.

questions.question: What do trees do for humans according to the passage?
questions.answer: They provide beneficial things that come as gifts from divine mercy.

questions.question: What lesson comes from the image of gardens producing many foods?
questions.answer: It teaches that one Lord brings forth many kinds of sustenance from the earth.

questions.question: Why is milk described in such an elevated way?
questions.answer: Because it is pure, nourishing, and mercifully provided through animals for human benefit.

questions.question: What happens to things when Allah’s name is mentioned, according to the passage?
questions.answer: They are made obedient and brought into service.

questions.question: What does the passage say, in meaning, to those who rely only on natural forces?
questions.answer: It tells them that the forces they trust are themselves controlled and cannot act independently.

questions.question: How are the rootlets like a sign seen in the life of Musa, peace be upon him?
questions.answer: They break through rock by Allah’s order just as rock was opened through a divinely commanded sign.

questions.question: How are leaves connected to the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him?
questions.answer: Their staying fresh under intense heat points to Allah’s power over fire and burning.

questions.question: What is the best summary of the argument in this passage?
questions.answer: The wonders of creation show that every part of nature works under Allah’s authority, mercy, and command.

questions.question: At the start of this passage, what earlier teaching is brought up again?
questions.answer: The teaching that all beings, through their created condition, declare dependence on Allah.

questions.question: How does the passage answer that teaching?
questions.answer: It answers by clearly affirming that it is true.

questions.question: What scene is used to make the point easier to understand?
questions.answer: A scene is imagined in which one man drives and commands the people of an entire town.

questions.question: Why would no one think that man acted only by himself?
questions.answer: Because the action is too broad and forceful for one person’s private ability.

questions.question: What official role is he compared to?
questions.answer: He is compared to a soldier carrying out authority from above.

questions.question: After this example, what broad claim is made about everything in creation?
questions.answer: Everything acts in Allah’s name and with power given by Him.

questions.question: What do the examples of seeds and grains teach about size and power?
questions.answer: They teach that a tiny cause can produce an enormous result only because Allah creates that result.

questions.question: What does the passage say, in meaning, about the work of trees?
questions.answer: Trees receive provision from divine mercy and hand it to us in useful forms.

questions.question: What does the image of gardens as cooking places suggest?
questions.answer: It suggests planning, preparation, abundance, and the production of many foods by Allah’s power.

questions.question: How do grazing animals become signs in this passage?
questions.answer: They provide pure milk, showing Allah’s mercy through familiar creatures.

questions.question: What surprising action of roots is emphasized?
questions.answer: They move through hard earth and stone even though they are delicate.

questions.question: What larger spiritual lesson should a believer take from that?
questions.answer: A believer should know that no obstacle is independent when Allah commands.

questions.question: Why does the passage speak so strongly against naturalist philosophers?
questions.answer: Because they ignore clear signs that created things are ruled by Allah, not by blind forces.

questions.question: What two Qur’anic prophetic examples are alluded to in the last part of the passage?
questions.answer: One refers to Musa, peace be upon him, and rock; the other refers to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and fire.

questions.question: How do those two examples help complete the message of the passage?
questions.answer: They show that even what seems strongest in nature, like stone and heat, is under Allah’s control.
